item.dc:creator: Marco Rossi
item.description: The rules surrounding speed limit signs are standard across the country, but how they're followed can vary. The rules, however, are fairly clear. The federal government doesn't set speed limits, even on interstates. Instead, states and local municipalities depend on traffic engineers to help decide posted speed limits.

The rules surrounding speed limit signs are standard across the country, but how they're followed can vary. The rules, however, are fairly clear. The federal government doesn't set speed limits, even on interstates. Instead, states and local municipalities depend on traffic engineers to help decide posted speed limits. Those are determined by considering laws, the areas where the speed limit will be posted, and the safety of the area, including the flow of traffic and frequency of accidents. (Not, though, the long-touted "85th-percentile rule." )

Traffic engineers often refer to their bible, the 1,100-page-plus Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices , written and revised by the Federal Highway Administration. If you're curious, turn to Page 84 of the revised 11th edition, where the section "Speed Limit Signs and Plaques" resides. The item to pay attention to is number 14: "Speed Limit (R2-1) signs, indicating speed limits for which posting is required by law, shall be located at points of change from one speed limit to another."

If you look at the lineage of Aston Martin's main production grand tourer over the years, it goes straight from the DB9 of the 2000s and early 2010s to the DB11 in 2016. Why did they seemingly just skip DB10? Is the number 10 unlucky in British culture? Turns out, A) it didn't and B) no. In fact, Aston Martin did indeed build a DB10; it just never made production.

A few years before the DB11 came along, work was underway on Daniel Craig's fourth James Bond movie, "Spectre." Director Sam Mendes, who helmed the wildly successful and, by most accounts, very good "Skyfall," was returning, and he wanted a new Aston Martin for Bond to drive. Enter the DB10, a car that was originally a concept sketch for the next Vantage , but became its own special model brought to life specifically for the movie. Fun fact: this was apparently the very first time an entirely new car was made for a Bond film.

Getting pulled over is never a fun time. The reasons are seemingly endless, from driving a police magnet to dangling a keepsake from the rearview mirror or having Flock misidentify your car as stolen . Now imagine going through any of these scenarios while also having a disability that creates communication challenges, such as autism. For someone with sensory, cognitive, and verbal difficulties, the already stressful event of being pulled over could lead to trauma or even being shot. And for the police officer, being unaware of the driver's medical condition can lead to miscommunication and mishandling of the situation.

That's why the Blue Envelope Program was developed: to improve communication between law enforcement and people who require additional accommodations or time during stops. Designed to be an all-inclusive information tool that's easy and straightforward to use for both the driver and officer, on the envelope's exterior are printed instructions and guidelines regarding how to interact with one another, while inside are essential documents, such as a driver's license, proof of insurance, and vehicle registration.

item.dc:creator: Tyler Brooks
item.description: It's probably been two decades since you've used a floppy disk — unless you're managing air traffic or preparing to launch intercontinental ballistic missiles. item.content:encoded:
Briefing: It's probably been two decades since you've used a floppy disk — unless you're managing air traffic or preparing to launch intercontinental ballistic missiles. The Federal Aviation Administration, a bit behind the technology curve, announced Thursday that it will finally phase out 3.5-inch floppy disks at air traffic control facilities.

It's probably been two decades since you've used a floppy disk — unless you're managing air traffic or preparing to launch intercontinental ballistic missiles. The Federal Aviation Administration, a bit behind the technology curve, announced Thursday that it will finally phase out 3.5-inch floppy disks at air traffic control facilities. The agency aims to rid itself of the antiquated technology by the end of 2028. In its place, air traffic controllers will have a modern, fully digitized system at their disposal.

The FAA plans to replace four legacy systems that date back to the 1980s with the Enterprise Information Display System (E-IDS) at 435 locations. The transition has already happened at Atlantic City International Airport, Nashville International Airport, Greater Rochester International Airport, and a pair of data processing hubs in Atlanta and Salt Lake City. School buses haven't changed much since 1939 , but they came a long way before then. Some of the first vehicles used to take kids to school were simply horse-drawn wagons. Fast-forward a few years and we find Crown Coach evolving the concept of motorized school buses even further. However, getting those mighty motors to turn over in the first place was no simple task, which is where the Buick Nailhead comes into play. It might not have directly powered the plane, but its earliest flights were only possible thanks to the engine.

A turbine engine requires a certain amount of airflow to ensure the fuel first ignites properly, and it has to reach a certain speed before the combustion process can sustain itself. As a result, the turbojet engines need to begin spinning even before they're operating on their own. But these are massive mills weighing in at 6,000 pounds each, so a simple electric starter like the one in a traditional car wouldn't have the strength to get the job done. A pair of Buick engines, on the other hand, would be enough to give its turbines the power they needed.

Esbjerg, Denmark, is using large electric heat pumps to extract heat from the North Sea and supply its district-heating network. During a two-hour winter test, seawater entered the system at 3.3°C and left at 1.2°C. The two heat pumps consumed 19.9 MW of electricity and supplied 55.2 MW of heat at a district-heating water temperature of 90°C. The difference, 35.3 MW, came from the seawater. The project team’s May 2025 operating report recorded a coefficient of performance, or COP, of 2.8. The figures describe that test, not annual average performance.

A heat pump transfers thermal energy from a colder source to a warmer destination. Its refrigerant absorbs heat at a temperature below that of the seawater, and an electrically driven compressor raises the temperature so the heat can enter the district network. Esbjerg uses carbon dioxide as its refrigerant in a high-pressure cycle. For each unit of electricity used by the compressors during the test, the plant delivered 2.8 units of heat. Resistance heating would have required 2.8 times as much electricity for the same heat output under those conditions.

For any savvy driver reluctant to cough up the eye-wateringly steep new-car asking prices today, a used car seems like a no-brainer option. However, buying a used car can be a minefield, too. Inspect the car too casually, and you could be flirting with unreliability. Luckily, the non-profit organization Consumer Reports (CR) helps buyers identify the vehicles that are much more likely to suffer unexpected faults or hidden issues — like burning oil in the case of gas-powered cars.

For those wondering, your car burning oil means oil is getting into the combustion chamber where it gets burned along with the air-fuel mixture. And since oil is essential for lubrication, cooling, and protecting the internal components inside the engine, your car burning or using too much oil can have serious consequences for its longevity. Naturally, this problem will cause oil levels to run low, reducing the lubrication inside the engine — also known as oil starvation . Without an effective lubrication film, the friction between moving parts inside the engine can accelerate wear on critical components, which can ultimately result in complete engine failure.

Copper is no longer used on modern cars because it wears out relatively quickly inside a cylinder of exploding gas that can routinely exceed 2,000 degrees Fahrenheit in normal operation. It feels like trucks get bigger and bigger every year. The differences between modern trucks and their predecessors are abundantly clear when you look at something like a Ford F-150 from the 1970s alongside a modern version: cabs are getting longer, beds are getting shorter, and footprints keep expanding. This is, in part, the result of George W. Bush-era revisions to the Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) standards, which linked each truck's fuel-economy target to its footprint, holding bigger trucks to lower mpg targets.

While some automakers have abandoned the compact and midsize truck segments, the ones still going strong are pretty impressive. In particular, the Ford Maverick is nearly the perfect truck , even with its un-trucklike unibody design. And if its excellent hybrid fuel efficiency, spiffy handling, user-friendly tech, and agreeable ride don't sell it for you, then maybe some of its hidden features will.
